# What celld guarantees

celld makes two promises about your data. Exactly one node serves a cell
at a time, so two machines never write the same database. And celld does
not answer a write until that write survives a failure, so nothing you
were told succeeded is lost.

This page is how both promises are kept. Fencing is the part that keeps
the first one true when a node is slow, paused, or cut off from the
network: celld refuses that node's writes rather than trusting it to
notice it lost the cell. Both claims rest on the object
store, so this page starts with what you must provide: a bucket with
working conditional writes, and a supervisor that restarts the process.
The mechanism follows, so you can check the argument against the code.

## What the bucket must provide

celld needs three properties from the object store:

- A conditional create: the write must fail when the object exists.
- A conditional overwrite: the write must fail when the object changed
  after the read.
- Read-after-write consistency: a read after a successful write must
  return that write.

The qualified stores are Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Tigris, Google Cloud
Storage, and Azure Blob Storage. celld's release tests run against R2,
and the S3 path uses the same client and the same headers.

Backblaze B2, Hetzner Object Storage, and DigitalOcean Spaces do not
implement the required conditional writes. celld is not correct on such
a store: two nodes can then own one cell. A store can also accept the
conditional headers and ignore the condition, and that store fails late
and silently — so run the storage test below.

MinIO (the community edition) implements the conditional writes and
passes the storage test, but celld has not qualified it for production.
One release is broken: RELEASE.2025-09-06T17-38-46Z answers the
conditional create of an absent object with `NoSuchKey`, so the first
deploy fails (denoland/celld#162). Use RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z or
later.

The request dialect differs per provider. An S3-compatible bucket gets
the `If-None-Match: *` and `If-Match` headers, and the condition
compares the etag. A `gs://` bucket selects the Cloud Storage XML API
with the `x-goog-if-generation-match` precondition and OAuth
credentials, because Cloud Storage does not apply `If-Match` to a PUT.
An `az://` bucket (the NAME is the container) uses the same `If-`
headers, which Put Blob applies. The adapter treats `AlreadyExists` and
`Precondition` (HTTP 412 on Azure) as clean conditional-write
rejections and keeps every other error ambiguous, because an ambiguous
write can have changed the object.

Azure was qualified on 2026-08-18 under an account key, a VM managed
identity, and an AKS workload identity, single-node. A managed identity
on Azure App Service or Azure Container Apps does not work; see
[limitations](limitations.md).

## The storage test

No store publishes these properties, so celld asks the store directly.
The command `celld diagnose` sends four conditional writes to your
bucket and reports the result:

```
ok bucket conditional write (create, reject-create, update, reject-stale)
```

Two of the four writes must fail. A store that accepts either one
cannot fence a cell, so celld names the store as the fault and the
command exits with an error. Each node repeats the test once at
startup, and a node that finds a broken store stops. Set
`CELLD_STORAGE_PROBE=0` to disable the startup test, or run
`celld diagnose --read-only` with a credential that cannot write.

The test writes and deletes one small object under `probe/`. A process
that stops mid-test can leave the object behind; it is small, and celld
never reads it. celld reserves `probe/` together with `cells/`,
`nodes/`, `node-cells/`, `fleet/`, `deploy/`, `deploy-blobs/`, `wake/`,
and `telemetry/`, and it deletes objects under some of them, so an
application must not write under any of these prefixes.

celld does not require a ranged read today, so a store that ignores the
`Range` header can still run a fleet.

## The supervisor

You must run celld under a supervisor that restarts the process, such
as systemd, Docker with a restart policy, or Kubernetes. A node fences
itself when it loses its lease (the mechanism is below), and a fenced
process exits; without a restart, the fleet loses that capacity until
an operator intervenes.

The supervisor must restart without an attempt limit, and it must wait
at least one lease lifetime between attempts. A node that cannot
acquire a lease at startup retries and does not exit, so a repeated
fence needs a node that acquires a lease and then loses it, and the
wait keeps that cycle slow enough to observe.

## The mechanism

The short version: the ownership records use conditional writes, so two
nodes cannot acquire one cell. The replicated data carries its fencing
epoch in the object key, so a node that lost ownership writes only into
a superseded prefix. And before celld acknowledges a write, it proves
the write durable and confirms that it still owns the cell.

### The ownership record

Each cell has one ownership record in the bucket. The record names the
owner node's session and carries a fencing epoch. A node acquires a
cell with a conditional write — a create when no record exists, a
compare-and-swap on the previous record when one does — and the bucket
accepts one such write, so two nodes cannot acquire the same cell.

Every activation advances the epoch, a takeover and a local wake alike.
Each owner therefore replicates under a fresh epoch, and an epoch never
has two writers.

### The epoch prefix

The replicator copies each cell's SQLite data to the bucket under
`cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, with plain unconditional PUTs. The epoch
in the key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing,
but its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the
current lineage. (The tiering path can first combine segments from many
cells into a node bundle, and it drains each segment into its per-cell
prefix later.)

The prefix protects the new owner's data from stale writes. The next
two sections protect the durability promise.

### The acknowledgement rule (RPO=0)

A gate holds each write response until a durability proof covers the
write. After a bucket proof, celld reads the ownership record once and
acknowledges only if the record still names this node at this epoch. A
partitioned node can commit locally and replicate into its superseded
prefix, but the ownership read then shows the new owner, so celld does
not acknowledge the write. The check reads the record instead of
comparing a clock, so a paused process or a skewed clock cannot pass
it.

A fleet proof does not require this read. The owner sends each write to
one or two other nodes, which hold a copy of its recent writes; those
nodes are its followers, and the set of them is the ensemble. Every
follower must fsync the write, and a takeover seals the prior node-log
session before it restores, so the stale owner cannot complete another
fleet proof.

### The ensemble needs two nodes

A node picks its followers from the other nodes in the fleet, so it never
counts itself. One follower is enough, therefore a fleet needs two
running celld nodes before any node can complete a fleet proof.
`CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet` is the default, so a fleet of one node requests the
fleet posture and does not get it.

A node recruits up to two followers, so a fleet of three or more nodes holds
three copies of an acknowledged write. The ensemble keeps acknowledging while
one follower remains, therefore a fleet does not fall back to the bucket each
time it loses a follower.

A node without an ensemble stays correct. It acknowledges each write on a
bucket proof instead, so celld still does not acknowledge a write before a
durability proof covers it. The cost is latency: the write waits for the object
store, and an object store round trip is much slower than a follower fsync.

### The takeover recovery gate

The default fleet mode can acknowledge a write once the node-log
ensemble stores it; the bucket upload can complete later. Each process
session therefore creates a conditional node-log record before its
first fleet-durable acknowledgement.

A cold activation checks the prior owner's log records before it reads
the bucket. An absent record proves that the session never acknowledged
past the bucket, and a sealed record proves that recovery completed. An
open or recovering record makes the activation run recovery: it fences
the record with a compare-and-swap, seals the reachable followers,
uploads their retained segments and bundles into the per-cell prefixes,
and then marks the record sealed. The activation cannot restore until
this sequence completes.

### Full-prefix restore

A restore selects the newest epoch prefix that contains LTX data, and
it reads the full contiguous chain from transaction zero. celld no
longer writes an epoch seal object, and a legacy `e<epoch>.seal.json`
object does not limit the chain.

A fenced node can append an unacknowledged tail to an older prefix, and
a later restore can expose that tail. This does not violate the
contract, because a failed or absent acknowledgement does not prove
that the write is absent. The rule reads the full chain because a
node-log recovery or a bundle drain can add an acknowledged tail after
an earlier restore; a restore that stopped at the earlier cut would
hide that tail and lose acknowledged data.

### Self-fencing

Each node holds a lease in the bucket. The lease carries an expiry, and
the node renews it after one third of the lifetime (`CELLD_TTL_MS`,
default 10000 ms). A renewal that does not reach the bucket does not
fence the node, because the node retries while the published expiry has
not passed.

A node that cannot reach the bucket cannot renew and cannot replicate,
so it must not own cells. When its published expiry passes, it fences
itself: it stops each active cell, and it fails every request that it
has not completed. A node whose lease record another writer replaced or
removed fences at once, because that record proves the authority moved.

The fence writes nothing to the bucket. Each peer already reads the
lease as dead or replaced, so a peer can acquire the cells through the
ownership records. And a request is safe even before the fence runs,
because celld compares the current time against the published expiry
each time it routes a request.

A fenced node logs a line that starts with `SELF-FENCE:` and stops with
the exit code 3. celld reports other internal failures with the same
prefix and code, so the line names the cause. The fenced state is
terminal: only a restart returns the node to the fleet, through the
same cold-activation path that a peer failure uses.

The failure of a node is a normal input, not a recovery procedure; the
[testing page](testing.md) shows the kill tests that exercise this
path.

# Testing

celld makes three important promises:

- An acknowledged write is durable.
- A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
- Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
  same on celld.

We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
on live fleets.

## Conformance: two runtimes, one output

We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
runtime by accident.

The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
`celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
WebSockets, and lifecycle.

## Specification: exhaustive at small size

The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.

Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
specifications arrived; we repaired it.

Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
pinned failure.

The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.

The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.

## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules

The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.

Thus the coordination protocol is a
[pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.

A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

1: # celld documentation
2: 
3: celld is a stateful distributed system. It runs server-side JavaScript on
4: your machines, and it stores the long-term state in a bucket that you own:
5: S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage. The JavaScript
6: API follows the API of Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects.
7: 
8: In Cloudflare terms, a cell is a Durable Object: a small server with a
9: name and a private SQLite database. You make one cell for each user, each
10: document, each chat room, or each AI agent. A cell serves HTTP, holds
11: WebSocket connections, sets alarms, and makes outbound connections. Cells
12: share no database, so the application divides into cells from the start.
13: Each cell runs on one thread: a second request interleaves only while the
14: first awaits, and storage operations are synchronous and never interleave,
15: so the data in a cell stays consistent.
16: 
17: You run celld as one process on each machine. That process is a **node**,
18: and the nodes that share one bucket are a **fleet**. Any node can serve
19: any cell, so you add capacity by starting another node against the same
20: bucket.
21: 
22: A cell has the same states as a Durable Object. A **resident** cell is in
23: memory: it is **active** while it does work, and **idle** when it waits.
24: celld removes an idle cell from memory. A cell that then keeps its
25: hibernatable WebSocket clients, and stays on its node, is **hibernated**.
26: A cell that no node holds is **inactive**. An inactive cell is only an
27: object in the bucket, so it costs almost zero, and every cell starts in
28: this state.
29: 
30: A cell keeps no memory across these transitions, so the constructor
31: runs again on the next event. A hibernated cell wakes the same way a
32: cold start does, except that its WebSocket clients stay connected and
33: it stays on its node.
34: 
35: One 8 GB node holds 1,000 resident cells, so one resident cell costs
36: approximately $0.05 each month.
37: 
38: Exactly one node serves a cell at a time. The nodes do not elect a leader
39: or keep a membership list: a node claims a cell by writing a small record
40: to the bucket, and it writes that record with a condition the storage
41: enforces — the write succeeds only if nobody else changed the record
42: first. Object storage therefore decides who wins, and two nodes cannot
43: both claim the same cell. The claim expires unless the node keeps
44: renewing it, so a machine that dies releases its cells without anyone
45: having to declare it dead.
46: 
47: celld does not answer a write until the data survives a failure, so no
48: write you were told succeeded is ever lost. That guarantee is called
49: RPO=0, for a recovery point of zero.
50: 
51: How celld earns it depends on how many nodes you run. One node writes the
52: data to the bucket first, which costs one storage round trip. Two or more
53: nodes are faster: the node serving the cell sends each write to another
54: node as well, and answers as soon as that node has the data on its own
55: disk. celld uploads the data to the bucket afterwards, so the bucket
56: still holds the long-term state. Run two or more nodes if write latency
57: matters to you; a single node has nobody to send to, so every write waits
58: for the bucket. `CELLD_DURABILITY` selects this behavior and defaults to
59: `fleet`.
60: 
61: When a node stops, another node takes the cell over. It first collects
62: whatever the stopped node had not uploaded yet, so the takeover starts
63: from a complete history. The [guarantees](guarantees.md) page
64: gives the full mechanism and the exact properties that the bucket must
65: provide.
66: 
67: When an event sets an alarm before its response boundary, celld does not send a
68: successful response until a durable wake entry covers the alarm. celld does
69: not let a later `waitUntil` alarm delay another event's response.
70: 
71: ## What do you build with cells
72: 
73: A cell fits a workload that divides into named, stateful units:
74: 
75: - **Real-time applications.** A multiplayer game, a chat room, or a
76:   collaborative document is one cell. The cell holds the WebSocket
77:   connections and the state of one room, so the room needs no lock and
78:   no external message bus.
79: - **Agents.** Each AI agent is one cell. The cell holds the memory, the
80:   schedule, and the inbox of one agent in its own SQLite database. An
81:   inactive agent has no resident process, so a large agent fleet costs
82:   almost nothing between events.
83: - **Sharded web applications.** One cell for each user, each tenant, or
84:   each device shards the application from the start. The contention of
85:   one shared database does not appear, because no shared database
86:   exists.
87: 
88: ## Contents
89: 
90: - [What do you build with cells](#what-do-you-build-with-cells)
91: - [Install](#install)
92: - [Configure object storage](#configure-object-storage)
93: - [Deploy an application](#deploy-an-application)
94: - [Operate D1 and KV](#operate-d1-and-kv)
95: - [Start a node](#start-a-node)
96: - [Add nodes](#add-nodes)
97: - [Shut down and roll out a node](#shut-down-and-roll-out-a-node)
98: - [Diagnose a fleet](#diagnose-a-fleet)
99: - [List Durable Objects](#list-durable-objects)
100: - [Environment variables](#environment-variables)
101: - [Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md)
102: - [What celld guarantees](guarantees.md)
103: - [Limitations](limitations.md)
104: - [Security](security.md)
105: - [Telemetry](telemetry.md)
106: - [Testing](testing.md)
107: - [WebAssembly](wasm.md)
108: - [Rust library API](library-api.md)
109: 
110: ## Install
111: 
112: The installer downloads the `celld` binary. Replication runs inside the
113: celld process, so a node needs no external replicator.
114: 
115: ```sh
116: curl -fsSL https://celld.dev/install.sh | sh
117: ```
118: 
119: If the installer tells you, add `~/.local/bin` to `PATH`. To install one
120: exact release, set `CELLD_VERSION` to its tag, for example `v0.0.1`; to
121: go back, run the installer again with the previous tag. The releases are
122: on [GitHub](https://github.com/denoland/celld/releases), and each release
123: has a GitHub Actions build attestation: verify a downloaded file with
124: `gh attestation verify <asset> --repo denoland/celld`.
125: 
126: ## Configure object storage
127: 
128: For an S3-compatible bucket, celld uses the standard AWS credential
129: chain. On Amazon EKS, celld reads the Pod Identity credentials from the
130: injected environment variables and the authorization-token file. For
131: Cloudflare R2: create a bucket, create an S3 API token with access to
132: that bucket, and set these variables:
133: 
134: ```sh
135: export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
136: export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
137: export AWS_REGION=auto
138: export S3_ENDPOINT=https://ACCOUNT_ID.r2.cloudflarestorage.com
139: export CELLD_BUCKET=s3://YOUR-BUCKET
140: ```
141: 
142: For Google Cloud Storage, celld uses Application Default Credentials.
143: Create a bucket. Then authenticate with `gcloud auth application-default
144: login`, or point `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` at a service-account
145: key that has access to the bucket. Then set the bucket:
146: 
147: ```sh
148: export CELLD_BUCKET=gs://YOUR-BUCKET
149: ```
150: 
151: A `gs://` bucket takes no `S3_ENDPOINT` and no `AWS_*` credentials, and
152: celld ignores the storage region. On a Compute Engine instance, celld can
153: use the attached service account, but the access scopes of the instance
154: cap this credential, and the default scope permits only storage reads.
155: Create the instance with the `cloud-platform` scope, so the IAM role of
156: the service account controls the access.
157: 
158: For Azure Blob Storage, the bucket NAME is the container, and the
159: storage account comes from the environment. Create a container. Then
160: set the account and one credential:
161: 
162: ```sh
163: export AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME=YOUR-ACCOUNT
164: export AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_KEY=...
165: export CELLD_BUCKET=az://YOUR-CONTAINER
166: ```
167: 
168: celld accepts three Azure credential families — a storage account key, a
169: managed identity, and a workload identity — and you must configure
170: exactly one. A system-assigned managed identity needs only the account
171: name. A user-assigned managed identity needs exactly one selector among
172: `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_OBJECT_ID`, and `AZURE_MSI_RESOURCE_ID`,
173: because two selectors can name two different identities. An identity
174: must hold the Azure Blob data-plane permission to read, write, list, and
175: delete blobs; the built-in
176: [`Storage Blob Data Contributor`](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles#storage-blob-data-contributor)
177: role supplies it.
178: 
179: celld reads a managed identity from the Azure instance metadata service,
180: which an Azure VM and an AKS node supply. Azure App Service and Azure
181: Container Apps supply a different endpoint, so a managed identity does
182: not work there; use a workload identity or an account key instead. The
183: standard AKS workload identity environment (`AZURE_AUTHORITY_HOST`,
184: `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`)
185: works with the public authority host, `https://login.microsoftonline.com`,
186: with or without a trailing slash; celld rejects a sovereign or custom
187: host. celld also rejects each recognized Azure configuration variable
188: outside these families — another credential source, an endpoint override,
189: the OneLake endpoint — and it ignores an `AZURE_*` name that
190: `object_store` 0.12 does not recognize, because that name cannot change
191: the client.
192: 
193: An `az://` bucket takes no `S3_ENDPOINT` and no `AWS_*` credentials, and
194: celld ignores the storage region. celld qualifies an `az://` bucket for
195: a production fleet: the conditional-write contract and the multipart
196: upload path were tested against a live Azure account on 2026-08-18 (see
197: [guarantees](guarantees.md)). For local development against
198: Azurite, set `AZURE_STORAGE_USE_EMULATOR=true`; Azurite is a development
199: store, so celld does not qualify it for a fleet either.
200: 
201: The bucket credentials give full control of the fleet, so keep them
202: safe. The bucket contains the deployments, the SQLite replicas, the
203: ownership records, the node leases, and the peer-authentication secret.
204: 
205: A bucket value can add a key prefix: `s3://YOUR-BUCKET/PREFIX`. Every
206: object of the fleet then goes below `PREFIX/`, so two fleets can share one
207: bucket. A bucket value without a prefix keeps the objects at the root of
208: the bucket, therefore an existing fleet does not move its data.
209: 
210: The store must provide conditional writes and read-after-write
211: consistency, because the ownership records depend on them. Amazon S3,
212: Cloudflare R2, Google Cloud Storage, Tigris, and Azure Blob Storage
213: qualify; Backblaze B2, Hetzner, and DigitalOcean Spaces do not. MinIO
214: (the community edition) passes the storage test, but celld has not
215: qualified it for production; do not use RELEASE.2025-09-06T17-38-46Z,
216: which rejects the conditional create that the first deploy sends
217: (denoland/celld#162). See [what celld guarantees](guarantees.md) for the
218: exact requirements.
219: 
220: ## Deploy an application
221: 
222: If the project contains Worker code, install `esbuild` on `PATH`; an
223: asset-only project does not need it. Then run `celld deploy` from an
224: applicable Wrangler project:
225: 
226: ```sh
227: git clone https://github.com/denoland/celld
228: cd celld/examples/counter
229: celld deploy . \
230:   --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
231:   --endpoint "$S3_ENDPOINT" \
232:   --region "$AWS_REGION"
233: ```
234: 
235: `celld deploy` accepts module Workers, Durable Object bindings, service
236: bindings, variables, cron triggers, D1 databases, KV namespaces, Workflows,
237: WebAssembly modules, and static assets. An asset project can include a
238: Worker or be asset-only, and the asset functions include the assets
239: binding, HTML handling, not-found handling, worker-first routes,
240: `_headers`, and `_redirects`. If the Wrangler configuration contains an
241: unknown key, the deploy stops with an error. See the
242: [Cloudflare compatibility](cloudflare-compat.md) page for the complete
243: deployment boundary.
244: 
245: A running node does not restart for a new deployment. Each node reads
246: `deploy/current.json` every 30 seconds (`CELLD_DEPLOY_POLL_S`) and adopts
247: a new deployment in place, and `POST /reload` on the internal listener
248: makes a node adopt the pointer now. A node builds the new deployment
249: beside the one it serves, and then it switches new requests to the new
250: deployment in one step. A request that started on the previous deployment
251: finishes on it. A deployment that does not build leaves the current
252: deployment serving, and the node reports the failure in its log and in
253: the `/reload` response. `POST /reload` also rebuilds an unchanged
254: deployment, so an edit to `CELLD_VARS_FILE` takes effect without a
255: restart.
256: 
257: A Durable Object that is not resident runs the new deployment at its
258: next activation. A resident Durable Object moves to the new deployment
259: at a safe point: no request runs in it, no alarm handler runs in it, no
260: output waits for durability, and no regular WebSocket is open. A request
261: that arrives while the object moves waits for the new code. The move
262: keeps the object's storage, its epoch, and its hibernatable WebSockets,
263: and it does not read or write the bucket. An object that reaches no safe
264: point in `CELLD_DEPLOY_MAX_AGE_S` seconds (default 60) is forced: celld
265: cancels its running work and closes its regular WebSockets with code
266: 1012, which is what a Cloudflare deployment does to every object. A
267: value of 0 forces every resident object at the adoption. In this window,
268: a request on one deployment can call a Durable Object on the other, so
269: two adjacent versions must accept each other's calls. The `/state`
270: response reports the deployment a node serves, the deployments it still
271: drains, the objects that are moving, and the deployment each resident
272: object runs.
273: 
274: ## Develop an application locally
275: 
276: Run `celld dev` in a Wrangler project:
277: 
278: ```sh
279: celld dev
280: ```
281: 
282: The command opens a local object store, deploys the application, and starts
283: one celld node. It does not require Docker or a cloud bucket. The Worker
284: listener uses `http://127.0.0.1:9876` by default. Use `--port` to select a
285: different port:
286: 
287: ```sh
288: celld dev --port 3000
289: ```
290: 
291: Use `--host` to select the Worker listener interface:
292: 
293: ```sh
294: celld dev --host 0.0.0.0
295: ```
296: 
297: A non-loopback IP exposes the Worker listener to the network. The internal
298: operator listener stays on loopback, so another machine cannot use its
299: operator API.
300: 
301: The default display uses color to identify each status and the application
302: URL. It hides the node warning and information logs, so the errors and the
303: listener remain easy to find. Use `--logs` to show these logs:
304: 
305: ```sh
306: celld dev --logs
307: ```
308: 
309: Set `NO_COLOR` to disable color. Set `FORCE_COLOR` to enable color when
310: the output is not a terminal. `NO_COLOR` always takes priority when both
311: variables are set.
312: 
313: You can also give the command a project directory or a Wrangler
314: configuration file:
315: 
316: ```sh
317: celld dev ./examples/counter
318: ```
319: 
320: The command stores the local objects and the celld work files in `.celld/dev`
321: below the project directory. Add `.celld/` to the application's `.gitignore`
322: file. A normal shutdown keeps this directory, so the next invocation uses the
323: same durable application state. Delete `.celld/dev` while `celld dev` is
324: stopped to reset that state.
325: 
326: The command does not expose the local object store through a fleet flag. A
327: regular node or an operator subcommand must use a supported cloud bucket.
328: 
329: The command watches the project directory. A source or configuration
330: change builds a new deployment and restarts the local node. The current
331: application continues to run during the build, and a failed build does
332: not replace it. The restart retains the durable application state.
333: 
334: The watcher ignores `.celld`, `.git`, `node_modules`, and `target`
335: directories at each depth. It does not watch a source file outside the
336: project directory. Worker projects need `esbuild` on `PATH`, and
337: asset-only projects do not need it.

339: ## Operate D1 and KV
340: 
341: `celld d1` runs SQL and migrations against a deployed D1 database. The
342: command uses the fleet bucket to find a node, and the node routes the
343: operation to the database cell.
344: 
345: ```sh
346: celld d1 migrations apply ledger --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET"
347: ```
348: 
349: `celld kv` reads and writes a deployed KV namespace. The bulk commands use
350: the Wrangler file format, so `wrangler kv bulk get` can export data for
351: `celld kv bulk put`.
352: 
353: ```sh
354: celld kv bulk put sessions wrangler-export.json --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET"
355: ```
356: 
357: `celld kv list` prints at most 1000 keys, because a namespace can hold
358: many more keys than an operator wants to read. The command reports on
359: stderr that more keys exist, and it gives the `--after KEY` that continues
360: the listing. Pass `--all` to read every key, or `--json` for one JSON
361: object per key.
362: 
363: Every celld command writes its data to stdout and its messages to stderr,
364: so a redirect or a pipe carries only data:
365: 
366: ```sh
367: celld kv list sessions --all --json --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" > keys.ndjson
368: ```
369: 
370: `celld --help`, `celld --version`, and the listener announcements use the same
371: stdout sink. The sink treats a closed pipe as a successful stop, and it reports
372: all other write and flush errors.

374: ## Start a node
375: 
376: For local development, the default listener is sufficient:
377: 
378: ```sh
379: celld \
380:   --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
381:   --endpoint "$S3_ENDPOINT" \
382:   --region "$AWS_REGION"
383: ```
384: 
385: For a fleet node, bind the public and internal listeners separately. The
386: ingress can reach the public listener, and the other nodes can reach the
387: internal listener:
388: 
389: ```sh
390: celld \
391:   --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
392:   --endpoint "$S3_ENDPOINT" \
393:   --region "$AWS_REGION" \
394:   --listen 0.0.0.0:8080 \
395:   --internal-listen 10.0.0.12:8081 \
396:   --advertise node-a.internal:8081
397: ```
398: 
399: An explicit advertised address requires an explicit internal-listener
400: address: set both command-line options, or their equivalent environment
401: variables. celld also rejects an explicit non-loopback public listener
402: without an explicit internal listener, because that shape identifies an
403: obsolete one-listener configuration.
404: 
405: celld cannot verify that an advertised hostname or a translated port
406: reaches the internal listener. You must route the advertised address to
407: the internal listener, and you must not route it to the public Worker
408: listener.
409: 
410: ## Add nodes
411: 
412: Start each node with the same bucket settings. Give each internal listener
413: a different address that the other nodes can reach, and set `--advertise`
414: to that address. The nodes find each other through the leases in the
415: bucket; there is no join command and no fixed membership list.
416: 
417: The bucket supplies discovery and authority, not network reachability.
418: Cell fetch and RPC traffic has a protocol version but has no content
419: signature, so the private network and its code are the security boundary.
420: Peer-control and reserved-cell operator requests use the fleet HMAC, but celld does not
421: terminate TLS. Put the advertised addresses on a private network that you
422: trust, or use an encrypted overlay such as WireGuard or Tailscale. The
423: internal listener also has an unauthenticated operator API, so it must not
424: reach the public internet. See the [security](security.md) page for the
425: complete boundary.
426: 
427: ## Shut down and roll out a node
428: 
429: celld shuts a node down gracefully on SIGTERM or SIGINT, the signals that
430: `systemctl stop`, `docker stop`, and a Kubernetes pod delete send. The
431: `/.well-known/celld/health` path reports the node as unhealthy, so a load balancer
432: stops public routing to it. New public requests receive a 503 response,
433: and celld closes each connection so the client can retry on a healthy
434: node. The node finishes the public HTTP requests that it accepted before
435: shutdown, and it continues to accept versioned peer traffic for cells that
436: it has not handed off.
437: 
438: You must set a longer orchestrator stop grace, such as systemd
439: `TimeoutStopSec` or Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. The grace
440: must cover the drain-token wait, the expected complete handoff, and one
441: no-progress interval (the settings below). Otherwise, the orchestrator
442: can send SIGKILL before celld completes the handoff.
443: 
444: The handoff works in batches. The node reserves a batch of cells and
445: stops new local routes to them: an accepted request stays local until it
446: finishes, and a new request waits for the successor route. The node
447: proves the batch durable and tries to publish one full snapshot of each
448: closed database. The snapshot is an L9 object, so the successor does not
449: replay the complete transaction history. The remote L0 chain remains an
450: additive fallback. If the snapshot retry window expires, the node releases
451: the cell with this proven L0 chain. The node then releases each ownership
452: record and asks a
453: compatible peer to acquire it. The peer acknowledges after the ownership
454: update and keeps the cell dormant, so the handoff does not restore an
455: unused runtime; a later request starts the cell under the peer activation
456: limit. The donor starts the next batch after each acknowledgement.
457: 
458: Four settings pace this work. `CELLD_RELEASES` sets the maximum number
459: of complete handoffs in progress (default 8), covering activity
460: cancellation, the durability proof, the final snapshot, the ownership
461: release, and the successor update; `CELLD_ACTIVATIONS` limits the
462: demand-driven restore and startup work. `CELLD_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS` sets
463: the maximum interval without a completed handoff (default 25000). Each
464: successor acknowledgement starts the interval again, so a large handoff
465: can continue while it makes progress. `CELLD_SHUTDOWN_TOTAL_MS` sets a 40000 ms
466: default bound for the complete process stop. An orchestrator stop grace must
467: be longer than this bound, so celld can finish its local durability shutdown.
468: A same-node preserve operation uses the shorter drain value as its semantic
469: limit because it has no successor acknowledgements.
470: 
471: Simultaneous stop signals do not flood the surviving nodes. A draining
472: node claims a fleet drain token in the bucket before it releases cells,
473: so concurrent donors hand off one node at a time. A donor that cannot
474: claim the token within `CELLD_DRAIN_TOKEN_WAIT_MS` milliseconds (default
475: 30000; `0` disables the token) proceeds without it, because the
476: orchestrator grace is finite. The token is advisory: a dead holder's
477: claim expires, and a handoff without the token is still safe.
478: 
479: A fresh process also holds its first healthy response until the fleet is
480: settled. The process requires its live node lease, no active donor, and memory
481: below every pressure low watermark on each live node. It also requires a total
482: restore backlog no larger than one `CELLD_ACTIVATIONS` budget. The incumbent
483: ownership counts must remain within one equal successor share above the fleet
484: mean. A joining process can satisfy this condition when it advertises paced
485: handoff support and owns fewer cells than the busiest incumbent. The process
486: publishes this successor capacity before readiness, so an idle rollout can
487: repair the ownership distribution during the next donor handoff.
488: 
489: An older peer does not publish the low-watermark result, so the gate uses that
490: peer's pressure latch during a mixed-version update. An unreadable fleet or an
491: unsettled condition holds readiness for up to `CELLD_READY_FLEET_GATE_MS`
492: milliseconds (default 120000; `0` disables the gate). The process then reports
493: healthy with a `ready_gate_expired` event. After the first healthy response,
494: fleet state does not remove readiness again.
495: 
496: A deadline-cut handoff can leave a node-log recovery for the replacement.
497: One process reads and uploads that dead session, and the other processes wait
498: for its result. A waiting process can replace an unresponsive recovery after
499: 30 seconds, so a failed recovery cannot block the fleet permanently. A
500: recovery store error keeps the session unsealed, so a later recovery must read
501: every retained bundle before the replacement can restore the acknowledged
502: state.
503: 
504: The internal listener continues to accept `/state` requests during the
505: drain, and the response reports the handoff and restore counters. The
506: public health response identifies the active drain with a 503 status.
507: 
508: To roll out a new version, use the rolling update of your orchestrator:
509: stop each node with SIGTERM, wait for its replacement to report healthy,
510: then move to the next node. celld paces the cell handoffs inside each node
511: shutdown, and the first-readiness gate paces the update against fleet
512: recovery, so a deployer does not need a separate fleet-level handoff gate.
513: 
514: Some upgrades are exceptions:
515: 
516: - The upgrade from v0.1.0 to v0.2.0 must not be a rolling update. Stop
517:   every v0.1.0 node, then start the v0.2.0 nodes. Two changes require
518:   this: v0.2.0 nodes advertise the internal listener, so ownership
519:   records that v0.1.0 nodes wrote name an address that v0.1.0 peers can
520:   not follow to a v0.2.0 node; and v0.2.0 compacts replicated data into
521:   block objects that a v0.1.0 reader can not restore. A fleet must not
522:   mix the two versions.
523: - The upgrade from v0.2.1 to v0.3.0 can use a rolling update. v0.3.0
524:   changes the default durability from `bucket` to `fleet`: a single node
525:   keeps the v0.2.1 behavior, and a fleet of two or more nodes activates
526:   fleet replication automatically. Stage the v0.3.0 binary on every node,
527:   and restart one node at a time. A mixed fleet stays safe, but a v0.3.0
528:   node cannot replicate to a v0.2.x peer, so it acknowledges writes
529:   through the bucket and retries until the peer runs v0.3.0. Do not start
530:   a v0.2.x binary after that node runs v0.3.0 unless the shutdown log
531:   contains `node-log close: sealed epoch`. A graceful stop attempts this
532:   seal, but a stop under load can leave the record open, and a v0.2.x
533:   binary cannot read writes that wait in the replicated log or bundle
534:   objects — this downgrade can lose acknowledged writes.
535: - The upgrade from v0.3.0 to v0.4.0 must not use a rolling update. Stop
536:   every v0.3.0 node, and then start the v0.4.0 nodes. v0.4.0 moves every
537:   proxied cell call — the fetch, the RPC, and the WebSocket — onto one
538:   tunneled connection that carries plain HTTP, and the peer protocol
539:   refuses a different version, so the two versions cannot proxy calls to
540:   each other. v0.4.0 also stores each new large KV value under its ownership
541:   epoch and writes an epoch-qualified row reference. A v0.3.0 node cannot
542:   read that reference, so a mixed fleet can make a committed KV value
543:   unavailable. The tunnel establishment carries the version, so a later
544:   protocol change can negotiate instead of refuse.
545: 
546: The internal listener also provides an alpha operator API. `/state`
547: reports the node state, `POST /reload` adopts the deployment pointer now,
548: and `POST /shutdown` starts the same graceful
549: handoff. The `POST /shutdown?handoff=preserve` request prepares a clean
550: same-node reload and keeps the ownership records. A release can change
551: this API, so keep the operator tooling and the celld release together.
552: 
553: ## Diagnose a fleet
554: 
555: `celld diagnose` reads the node leases in the bucket and sends a probe to
556: each live peer. It does not take a lease, and it does not change
557: ownership.
558: 
559: ```sh
560: celld diagnose \
561:   --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
562:   --endpoint "$S3_ENDPOINT" \
563:   --region "$AWS_REGION"
564: ```
565: 
566: To probe only some nodes, use `--peer NODE_ID` one or more times. The
567: report identifies expired records, unsafe or incorrect advertised
568: addresses, peers that it cannot reach, authentication failures, and
569: protocol versions that do not agree.
570: 
571: Each node line also shows `restoring`: the count of cold routes that hold
572: an activation permit or wait for one (a capacity waiter already holds a
573: permit, so each cold route counts once). During a rolling update, wait
574: for every node to report `restoring=0` before you restart the next node,
575: so one restart's cold work finishes before the next restart removes more
576: warm capacity.

578: ## List Durable Objects
579: 
580: List the Durable Object instances in the bucket:
581: 
582: ```sh
583: celld cell list \
584:   --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
585:   --endpoint "$S3_ENDPOINT" \
586:   --region "$AWS_REGION"
587: ```
588: 
589: Each line is a `Class:ID` cell scope. The ID is the Durable Object ID: a
590: 64-character hash unless the application supplies its own name. Give a
591: class name to list only that class, and pass `--json` for one JSON object
592: per line. An instance appears after the first event reaches it, because
593: its owner then writes an ownership record to the bucket; an ID that an
594: application only derives does not appear.
595: 
596: The listing also shows celld's own cells. A D1 database, a KV namespace,
597: and a Workflow are each a cell in a reserved class, and their names start
598: with `__`. They hold real data in the bucket, therefore the command shows
599: them. The `--json` output marks each row with `"reserved": true` or
600: `false`, so a script can select one kind:
601: 
602: ```sh
603: celld cell list --all --json --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" |
604:   jq -r 'select(.reserved | not) | .scope'
605: ```
606: 
607: A storage request returns at most 1000 instances, so the command stops at
608: 1000 instances and writes this line to stderr:
609: 
610: ```
611: 1000 cells shown; more exist. Continue with --after Room:d99d9174b25e46310694dd931b47fbde70a7460bb7b210b546060651ea2ff6e0
612: ```
613: 
614: Pass that `--after SCOPE` to read the next 1000 instances, or use
615: `--limit N` for a different bound:
616: 
617: ```sh
618: celld cell list --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" \
619:   --after Room:d99d9174b25e46310694dd931b47fbde70a7460bb7b210b546060651ea2ff6e0
620: ```
621: 
622: Pass `--all` to read the whole listing in one command. This makes one
623: request for each 1000 instances, so it can take minutes on a large fleet;
624: the command reports its progress and its request count on stderr.
625: 
626: The order is the storage order, and `--after` continues from the last
627: instance printed, so a sequence of `--after` commands lists each instance
628: one time. An instance that an application creates during the sequence can
629: appear or not appear, because the listing is not a snapshot.
630: 
631: The command writes the instances to stdout and every message to stderr,
632: so a script reads only instance data:
633: 
634: ```sh
635: celld cell list --all --json --bucket "$CELLD_BUCKET" > cells.ndjson
636: ```
637: 
638: ## Hot-cell overload
639: 
640: celld admits a maximum of 64 concurrent fetch events for one Durable Object
641: or Queue broker. Set `CELLD_MAX_CELL_REQUESTS` to use a different positive
642: limit.
643: 
644: celld returns HTTP status `503` when the target reaches this limit, and it
645: does not start the excess event. The response contains `Retry-After: 1` and
646: `X-Celld-Overload: cell`, so the application can retry or reject the work.
647: A local or remote Queue owner uses the same status and headers when it refuses
648: producer admission. The Queue response body is
649: `{"error":"cell admission refused"}`. A fixed-rate client must count the
650: response as rejected work, so an immediate retry does not increase the
651: configured offered rate.
652: 
653: The runtime writes a `cell_overload_refused` log event when a target becomes
654: saturated. The event contains the cell scope, the node, the region, the
655: in-flight count, and the limit. Count these overload responses separately
656: from the transport errors and the application failures.
657: 
658: ## Environment variables
659: 
660: For the full list, run `celld -h`. This table shows the primary settings:
661: 
662: | variable | purpose |
663: | --- | --- |
664: | `CELLD_BUCKET` | The fleet bucket, and an optional key prefix. The same as `--bucket` |
665: | `S3_ENDPOINT` | The S3-compatible endpoint. The same as `--endpoint` |
666: | `AWS_REGION`, `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` | The storage region |
667: | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` | Explicit AWS credentials. The standard AWS credential chain is also available |
668: | `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY` | Google credentials for a `gs://` bucket. Application Default Credentials are also available |
669: | `AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME` | The storage account for an `az://` bucket. The bucket NAME is the container |
670: | `AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_KEY` | The storage account key. Do not combine it with an identity selector |
671: | `AZURE_AUTHORITY_HOST`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` | The standard AKS workload identity environment for an `az://` bucket. The authority must be the public Azure host |
672: | `AZURE_STORAGE_USE_EMULATOR` | Set to `true` to develop against Azurite. celld does not qualify Azurite for a production fleet |
673: | `CELLD_ADDR` | The public Worker listener. The same as `--listen` |
674: | `CELLD_INTERNAL_ADDR` | The peer and operator listener. The same as `--internal-listen` |
675: | `CELLD_ADVERTISE` | The internal address that peers can reach. The same as `--advertise` |
676: | `CELLD_UNSAFE_PUBLIC_ADVERTISE` | Set to `1` to permit a literal public IP in `CELLD_ADVERTISE`. This setting does not resolve a DNS name or restrict the internal listener |
677: | `CELLD_NODE` | An explicit node-session ID |
678: | `CELLD_WATCH` | The local work directory for SQLite and replication |
679: | `CELLD_ESBUILD` | The path of the esbuild executable |
680: | `CELLD_ACTIVATIONS` | The limit for concurrent cold-cell activations (default: the available CPU count or 128, whichever is smaller) |
681: | `CELLD_DEPLOY_POLL_S` | The interval in seconds at which a node reads the deployment pointer and adopts a new deployment in place (default: 30) |
682: | `CELLD_DEPLOY_MAX_AGE_S` | How long a resident Durable Object can keep the previous deployment's code after an adoption before celld forces the move (default: 60; 0 forces at once) |
683: | `CELLD_OPERATION_DEADLINE_MS` | The deadline for a non-restore operation (default: 15000) |
684: | `CELLD_WORKER_LOADER` | Bind a Worker Loader (Code Mode) at this `env` name. A Worker can then start isolates at runtime. Off unless set (experimental) |
685: | `CELLD_MAX_LOADED_WORKERS` | The limit for concurrent loaded workers (default: 256) |
686: | `CELLD_MAX_CELL_REQUESTS` | The concurrent fetch limit for one Durable Object or Queue broker (default: 64) |
687: | `CELLD_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES` | The body limit for a public Worker request or a direct Durable Object request (default: 1 GiB) |
688: | `CELLD_MAX_RESIDENT_CELLS` | The hard limit for resident cells, enforced at admission |
689: | `CELLD_MAX_RSS_MB` | The memory threshold for pressure shedding, applied to the greater of the allocator-adjusted RSS and the allocator-adjusted active cgroup working set (default: 80% of the available memory; 0 disables the threshold and the absolute cap) |
690: | `CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE` | The default is `1`, so celld proves each write durable before it acknowledges the write. Set `0` to remove the replication wait and accept possible loss of an acknowledged write |
691: | `CELLD_DURABILITY` | How celld proves a write durable before it answers. The default is `fleet`: the node serving the cell sends the write to one or two other nodes and answers once they hold it on disk, or once the bucket upload finishes, whichever comes first. This needs two or more nodes; a single node has nobody to send to, so every write waits for the bucket. Set `bucket` to always wait for the bucket |
692: | `CELLD_LOG_CAPTURE_WORKERS` | The limit for concurrent log-capture workers (default: 8) |
693: | `CELLD_LOG_PIPELINE` | The limit for fleet log rounds that can be in flight (default: 4) |
694: | `CELLD_LOG_HEDGE_MS` | The wait before a leader sends a second copy of a slow log append to a follower. The default is adaptive: celld derives the wait from the slowest recent append in the ensemble (4 times that append, at least 250 ms, and always below the eviction backstop), so a loaded fleet does not send copies for honest slow appends. Set a value to use a fixed wait in milliseconds, and set `0` to disable the second copy. An append is idempotent per sequence, so the copy is safe, and the leader uses the answer that arrives first and confirms |
695: | `CELLD_LTX_TRUNCATE_PAGES` | The WAL size, in pages, at which celld truncates an ordinary cell's WAL file at the next checkpoint (default: 128, a 512 KiB cap). A passive checkpoint does not shrink the WAL file, so each capture reads the stale region after a restart. The truncate keeps the read small. Queue cells use passive checkpoints because a truncate boundary emits a full database image. Set `0` to disable the truncate for all cells |
696: | `CELLD_LTX_COMPACTION` | The default is `1`: celld creates additive L1 objects, and a takeover reads tens of objects instead of thousands. Set `0` on every node of a mixed fleet until all nodes can read v0.5.2 block objects, because an old reader cannot take over a cell after its first L1 publication |
697: | `CELLD_LTX_COMPACTION_MIN_TXIDS` | The durable TXID distance that queues a background L1 attempt (default: 256) |
698: | `CELLD_LTX_COMPACTIONS` | The node-wide limit for concurrent background L1 attempts (default: 2). `CELLD_RELEASES` bounds final handoff snapshots |
699: | `CELLD_LTX_DURABILITY_TIMEOUT_SECS` | The deadline for a durability proof and the final snapshot retry window, in seconds (default: 10). A slow or busy object store can need a longer deadline for a large write burst |
700: | `CELLD_VAR_*`, `CELLD_VARS_FILE` | Worker variable overrides |
701: | `RUST_LOG` | The runtime log filter |
702: 
703: The help output also shows the advanced tuning switches and their
704: defaults.
705: 
706: An unset variable selects its documented default. A Boolean variable
707: accepts only `0` or `1`. celld exits during startup when a supplied value
708: is invalid.
